documentation.range: The Sperm Whale has a large geographic range (Rice 1989). It has been documented in nearly all marine regions, from the equator (e.g. Eguiguren et al. 2021) to near the ice edges in high latitudes; for instance 75°N in Baffin Bay (Posdaljian et al. 2022) and 73°S in the Ross Sea (Giorli and Pinkerton 2023). The Sperm Whale is generally found in continental slope or oceanic waters, usually, but not always, deeper than 500 m. The distribution extends to many enclosed or partially-enclosed seas, such as the Mediterranean Sea, Sea of Okhotsk, Gulf of California, and Gulf of Mexico. However, Sperm Whales seem to be absent from the Red Sea and Black Sea, which have shallow sills. Male Sperm Whales can be found in ice-free waters at almost any latitude, but females and juveniles are largely restricted to tropical and sub-tropical waters, usually with sea-surface temperatures 15°C (Rice 1989), although there are exceptions (e.g. Posdaljian et al. 2024).
documentation.population:
During the later phases of the whaling era, sperm whaling was managed on the basis of geographically-delineated stocks (Donovan 1991). However, these stock divisions had little biological support (Dufault et al. 1999). Global genetic analyses found that geographic philopatry and social philopatry both influence genetic structure in the Sperm Whale, but much more so in females than males (Alexander et al. 2016). There is also cultural structure to female Sperm Whale populations, but these cultural divisions are not geographically distinct (Hersh et al. 2022). Thus, the global Sperm Whale population is not easily classified into largely separate populations. An exception is the subpopulation in the Mediterranean Sea which appears genetically and culturally isolated from Sperm Whales elsewhere (Rendell and Frantzis 2016), and has been assessed separately (Pirotta et al. 2021).

Following the end of most commercial whaling in the early 1980s, Sperm Whale population densities and sizes have been assessed in a number of ocean areas (mainly Northern Hemisphere), using line transect data from ship surveys (both visual and acoustic) and aircraft, as well as mark-recapture analyses of photoidentifications of individuals (e.g. Barlow and Taylor 2005, Gordon et al., 2020, Rinaldi et al. 2021).

Estimated Sperm Whale densities from the line transect surveys varied between 1.15–10.55 whales/1,000 km2, with a mean of 2.31 whales/1,000 km2 (Whitehead and Shin 2022). Extrapolating these densities to unsurveyed areas using oceanographic predictor variables gave an estimated global population of 736,053 (CV 0.218) Sperm Whales in 1993 (the mean year of the surveys) (Whitehead and Shin 2022).

Using a 5-parameter demographic model, the generation length of Sperm Whales in pre-disturbance conditions has been estimated at 31.9 years (Taylor et al. 2007).

Whitehead and Shin (2022) used a theta-logistic population model enhanced to simulate spatial structure and the non-removal impacts of whaling, and estimated annual whaling catches to produce a global population trajectory from 1710 (before commercial sperm whaling started) to 2022. A particularly important parameter in this model is the maximum potential rate of increase of the Sperm Whale, assumed to be 0.96%/year (Chiquet et al. 2013), a low value driven by the slow life history of the species. The model suggests a pre-whaling population of 1,949,698 which was substantially reduced by whaling (especially between 1810–1860 and 1950–1975) and then recovered, but not significantly, to about 844,761 in 2022 (Whitehead and Shin 2022; Supplementary information Figure 1). This model has been extended to 2025, and used to calculate the proportional change in population size between 1929–2025, i.e. over the last three generations (H. Whitehead, unpublished). This proportional decline was 0.483 (almost the same as the 0.482 in Whitehead and Shin's (2022) original analysis). Of 1,000 runs with randomly chosen values of demographic parameters (from reasonable prior distributions), the 95% confidence interval for this proportional decline was 0.243–0.690. Forty-four per cent of these runs with randomly chosen parameters had a proportional decline 0.5, the criterion for "Vulnerable" under A1(d). While there is clearly uncertainty about the three-generation decline, little is due to the estimated generation length, as the global population appears to have been somewhat stable between 1920–1945 (Whitehead and Shin 2022; Supplementary information Figure 1). However, this model assumes that, apart from the direct and indirect effects of whaling, populations recovered at the maximum potential rate of increase.

There have been several estimates of trends in Sperm Whale population numbers for particular areas since 1978 (i.e. following the end of most commercial whaling) from either repeated visual surveys from ships or aircraft or mark-recapture photoidentification studies spanning at least 10 years (see Whitehead and Shin 2022). These are the trends that were either calculated in the cited paper, or from data presented:
· Antarctic males (1978–1998, ship visual (Branch and Butterworth 2001)): +1.9%/year

· California current (1991–2014, ship visual (Moore and Barlow 2017)): +0.9%/year

· Eastern tropical Pacific (1986–2000, ship visual (Gerrodette and Forcada 2002)): -4.9%/year

· Gulf of California (2009–2018, ship surveys (Pérez-Puig et al. 2024)): -50.6%/yr, attributed to a collapse in the population of Dosidicus gigas, the Sperm Whales’ primary prey in the area

· Gulf of Mexico (2003–2018, ship visual (Garrison et al. 2020)): -4.2%/year

· Hawaiian islands (2002–2017, ship visual (Bradford et al. 2021)): +0.1%/year

· Galápagos islands (1985–1995, ship visual (Whitehead et al. 1997)): -9.0%/year

· Galápagos islands (1985–1995, photoidentification (Whitehead et al. 1997)): -20.0%/year

· Lesser Antilles (2001–2013, photoidentification (Rinaldi et al. 2021): -6.2%/year

· Lesser Antilles (2005–2015, photoidentification (Gero and Whitehead 2016)): -19.5%/year

· New Zealand males (1993–2016, photoidentification (Somerford et al. 2022)): -3.1%/year

Although there is much uncertainty, these estimates of trends can be grouped as follows (Whitehead and Shin 2022):

a) Substantial decline in years following heavy whaling likely due to lingering disruptions of the sex ratio and social structure (Eastern tropical Pacific; Galápagos islands).

b) Substantial declines in areas with high human impact, such as the Gulf of Mexico and Lesser Antilles. The Gulf of California decline noted above may also be placed in this group (especially if the collapse of the Humboldt Squid, Dosidicus gigas, an important prey item for Sperm Whales, can be linked to anthropogenic effects such as fishing or climate change), as might evidence for declines in the Mediterranean (e.g. Frantzis et al. 2019).

c) Small increases in areas with low human impact (California current, Hawaiian Islands), and especially among the males in the Antarctic which had previously been heavily reduced by whaling. However, there seem to have been declines in male abundance off Australia (1965–1978 (Carroll et al. 2014)) and New Zealand (1991–2017(Somerford et al. 2022)).
These trend estimates strongly suggest that, following whaling, not all populations have rebuilt at the maximum potential rate of increase, and some have declined. The declines in the eastern tropical Pacific may be an indirect consequence of whaling (included in Whitehead and Shin's (2022) model), but most of those elsewhere are likely driven by other threats. Thus, the proportional three-generation decline is likely greater than the 0.483 estimated from the model.

Upper: Estimated trajectories of global Sperm Whale population using best estimates for model parameters in red, and 20 trajectories using randomly chosen but reasonable parameter estimates in black. Lower: Reported annual global Sperm Whale catch. (From Whitehead and Shin 2022).
documentation.habitats: Sperm Whales can be found in almost all marine waters deeper than 500 m that are not much covered by ice, except in the Black Sea and Red Sea (Rice 1989, Whitehead 2003). In some areas, for instance in the western North Atlantic, Sperm Whales, especially males, can occur in shallower waters (e.g. Scott and Sadove 1997). Females and young are usually restricted to waters at latitudes lower than about 40–50º and to areas where sea surface temperatures are greater than about 15ºC (Rice 1989), although there are exceptions (e.g. Posdaljian et al. 2024). Sperm Whales are generally more numerous in areas of relatively high primary productivity (Jaquet et al. 1996), although there are some exceptions, such as the Sargasso Sea (Wong and Whitehead 2014) and the central North Pacific gyre (Barlow and Taylor 2005). The principal foods of the Sperm Whale are mesopelagic and bathypelagic squid which they catch during deep (ca. 350–1,200 m) dives lasting about 45 minutes (Clarke et al. 1993, Kawakami 1980, Watwood et al. 2006). Most of these prey are small and slow-moving, such as the Histioteuthis family of squids (ca. 400g). However, Sperm Whales do take much larger and more active squid such as the Humboldt Squid Dosidicus gigas (50 kg), while large males in the Antarctic catch and eat the Colossal Squid Mesonychoteuthis hamiltoni (500 kg). Sperm Whales, especially males, also take fish, such as benthic sharks (Kawakami 1980, Rice 1989). It is generally believed that the Sperm Whale's only serious natural predator is the Killer Whale (Orcinus orca). Killer Whales do sometimes catch and kill Sperm Whales (Pitman et al. 2001), but it is unknown how frequently this predation is successful. Although Sperm Whales are afflicted by parasites and diseases, few seem lethal (Lambertsen 1997). Sperm Whales mass strand in various parts of the world. Numbers in a stranding range to over 100, although there are usually fewer (Evans et al., 2002). The strandings include various combinations of males, females and young, and most animals seem healthy on stranding. The whales can be clustered within a few hundred metres of shoreline, or spread over tens of kilometres (Evans et al. 2002), and the temporal span of their arrivals at the shore can range from minutes to days. Many, probably most, stranded Sperm Whales die. The causes of mass strandings are not clear, likely vary, and may or may not include anthropogenic factors (Mazzariol et al. 2011). While spectacular, mass strandings probably total a few thousand or fewer individuals per year and are not a major impact on the global Sperm Whale population.
documentation.threats:
Although threats vary across the nearly global range of this species, the most serious threats to the species are:

Shipping. Sperm Whales are hit by ships (Laist et al. 2001, Nisi et al. 2024). As most strikes likely take place well offshore, the global severity of this threat can only be inferred (Nisi et al., 2024), but in some areas where shipping routes and important Sperm Whale habitat coincide, mortality from ship strikes is considered unsustainable (Fais et al. 2016, Frantzis et al. 2019).

Bycatch. Sperm Whales are incidentally caught or entangled in a variety of fisheries in many areas (e.g. Haase and Félix 1994, Hamer et al. 2012). Sperm whales have been considered as being at moderate risk (relative to other cetacean species) from bycatch in demersal gillnets, demersal long-lines, pelagic trawls, and demersal trawls, although some experts judged that this risk may have been overestimated (Brown et al. 2013).

Chemical pollution. A range of contaminants have been found in Sperm Whales including persistent organic pollutants (Pinzone et al. 2015), flame retardants (Zaccaroni et al. 2018) and trace elements such as arsenic (Savery et al. 2014). These may have important health effects (Pinzone et al. 2015, Zaccaroni et al. 2018).

Plastics. Sperm Whales ingest marine debris, especially macroplastics, at a seemingly higher rate than most other cetaceans (Fossi et al. 2020). This likely relates to visual and acoustic similarities between their natural cephalopod prey and plastic debris, as well as to their use of suction feeding (Fossi et al. 2020). The incidence of marine litter in the stomachs of stranded Sperm Whales varies between seas and oceans, with a high of 74% in the Mediterranean Sea to a low of 4% in the Pacific (Fossi et al. 2020). Fishing-related debris (e.g., ropes and nets) can constitute a considerable proportion of the gut contents of necropsied Sperm Whales (Jacobsen et al. 2010, Unger et al. 2016). Macroplastic items can physically block the digestive tract of Sperm Whales and lead to death (e.g. De Stephanis et al. 2013). Microplastics (<5 mm), which contain, or may absorb, a wide range of toxic chemicals, are also an important threat to aquatic mammals (Nabi et al. 2022). Microplastics have been detected in the gut and tissues of Dosidicus gigas, a major prey of Sperm Whales in the Eastern Pacific Ocean (Alfaro-Núñez et al. 2021, Gong et al. 2021). However, there is currently much less information on the occurrence and effects of microplastics than macroplastics specifically in the case of Sperm Whales.

Noise. In recent years, there has been increasing evidence that anthropogenic underwater sound from seismic operations, naval operations, shipping, and other sources can be harmful to cetaceans (Weilgart 2017). Effects can range from masking of important sounds, behavioural disruption (including of vocalizations), temporary or long-term displacement, increased stress or energy expenditure, to permanent hearing damage or fatal strandings (Weilgart 2017). Thus, the negative effects of underwater noise on the health of individual animals and their populations can be chronic or acute. For Sperm Whales, there is evidence of behavioural change due to vessel noise (Azzara et al. 2013) and seismic airgun noise (Miller et al. 2009), as well as displacement and/or changes in behaviour during naval exercises (Isojunno et al. 2016, Stanistreet et al. 2022). However, some studies have found only subtle effects of loud impulsive noises (e.g. Miller et al. 2009). Thus, quite extensive research shows that Sperm Whales can be negatively impacted by underwater noise, but the potential impact on population dynamics is unclear.

Climate change. The effects of global climate change on the marine environment are likely to affect Sperm Whales, although the nature and severity of impacts are unclear (Learmonth et al. 2006). Sperm whales feed at depth where increases in temperature will generally be delayed (Levin and Bris 2015. They also breathe at the surface in waters where they tolerate sea-surface temperatures ranging from 0–30°C. Thus, direct effects of temperature increase in the oceans are less likely to be important for Sperm Whales than indirect effects due to changes in oceanic productivity, prey abundance and ecosystem functioning arising from climate change (see Levin and Bris 2015). Particularly, changes in the distribution and abundance of Sperm Whale prey, compounded by overfishing, may impact Sperm Whale distribution, foraging success, and overall fitness (Eguiguren et al. 2025, Pérez-Puig et al. 2024). This is illustrated by the decrease in calf production 1–2 years following a sea temperature rise (Whitehead 1997).

In some areas, there are additional threats that may be locally serious, including:

Tourism. In some parts of the world, especially off islands with deep waters close to the coast, Sperm Whales are regularly sighted close to shore, and in these places they may be threatened by disturbance from unregulated or poorly-regulated tourism (Barteneva-Vitry et al. 2025).

Whaling. The catches by Japan in its coastal waters and off Lamalera, Indonesia are small (some tens per annum; see above) by historical standards, and in the case of Lamalera, not well documented. These catches target a very small part of the global population of Sperm Whales, but may have some local impact.

Persecution following depredation. Sperm Whales that depredate fisheries are sometimes persecuted, by ramming, shooting or explosives to deter the depredation (Hucke-Gaete et al. 2004). It is currently not possible to assess the extent or impact of this practise.
documentation.measures: The species is on Appendix I of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES) and Appendices I and II of the Convention on Migratory Species (CMS).<span lang="EN-GB"> CMS adopted a Concerted Action for eastern tropical Pacific Sperm Whales in 2017, proposing collaborative efforts to address cultural dimensions in conservation. The International Whaling Commission is nominally responsible for managing the exploitation of Sperm Whale populations under the International Convention for the Regulation of Whaling. The Schedule of the Convention lists Sperm Whale whaling seasons, Sperm Whale size limits and Sperm Whale catch limits (0 at present). It also designates sanctuaries for all whale species in the Indian and Southern Oceans. However, no specific scheme is in place for conserving Sperm Whale populations and managing the human activities that affect them. Moreover, many range states are not members of the International Whaling Commission, and therefore are not bound by its regulations. Many range states have adopted measures, such as marine protected areas, and regulations affecting fishing, shipping and tourism activities that provide some protection to Sperm Whales. However, no formal protection or enforcement capabilities exist for Sperm Whales when they are outside national jurisdictions.
documentation.use_trade: The commercial value of the animal (a function of its size and the quality of Sperm Whale oil) drove two massive worldwide hunts: the technologically primitive "open-boat" hunt from 1712–~1920 (Best 1983, Starbuck 1878), and modern whaling using engine-driven whaling ships and harpoon guns from ~1910–1988 (Tønnessen and Johnsen 1982). Since 1988, the International Whaling Commission has received reports of 0–10 animals per year caught in Japanese waters by modern methods, and 4–43 per year off Lamalera, Indonesia, by traditional methods (https://iwc.int/management-and-conservation/whaling/total-catches).
documentation.rationale:
The species was classified as Vulnerable (VU) on the IUCN Red List in 2008. The Mediterranean subpopulation was classified as Endangered (EN) in 2012.

The criterion for Vulnerable (VU) status under A1(d) is at least a 50% population reduction in three generations. A model estimating the historical trajectory of global Sperm Whale abundance estimated a three generation decline of 48.3% using best-supported parameter values, just less than the threshold for Vulnerable. Forty-four per cent of model runs with credible parameter values estimated a three generation proportional decline 0.5. The model only included the direct and indirect effects of whaling, but trend estimates for specific areas during the post-whaling period found that decreases were more frequent, and greater in magnitude, than increases. Most of these recent declines are likely driven by non-whaling threats, which are generally increasing in magnitude. The Red List Guidelines state that precaution should be used. Therefore, a decline of at least 50% in three generations is likely, once the effects of modern non-whaling threats are considered. Thus, this species is assessed as Vulnerable (VU) under A1(d).
documentation.taxonomic_notes: Although Physeter catodon is still occasionally used in the literature, P. macrocephalus is recommended (Rice 1989). Both names are listed on the same page of the original description by Linnaeus (1758), and priority is unclear. However, P. macrocephalus is preferable because it is used much more frequently, and this will support nomenclatural stability.
